transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thank you for seeing me. It’s, uh, it's kind of hard to explain where to start, but I guess what really brought me in today is... well, it usually happens at night. I work as a cashier, which, you know, isn't exactly what I thought I'd be doing at 42 with a bachelor's degree, so the days can be pretty draining. You stand there for hours, ringing people up, dealing with all sorts of attitudes, and by the time I get home, or maybe after I've had a really tense dinner—sometimes dinners just get so stressful, you know how it is—I just... I start eating. 

And I know a lot of people probably snack to unwind after a long shift, but this isn't really like that. It’s like... it feels like the whole decision-making part of my brain just completely shuts off. I'll be there in the kitchen, and it’s almost like I'm watching myself from the outside. I can literally see my own hand reaching for more food, grabbing something else from the cupboard or the fridge, and I'm thinking in my head that I should stop, but I just can't make myself do it. I can't stop. It’s the strangest, most frustrating feeling, because I am aware of what I'm doing, but the brakes are just totally gone. And it just keeps happening on these tense nights, so I finally thought I needed to come in and talk to someone about it, because I just don't understand why I can't just tell myself no and have it actually work, you know?
Do you usually feel guilty or ashamed after one of these eating episodes?

Guilty? Oh, God, yes. It's... it's actually overwhelming, the amount of guilt I feel. And shame, definitely shame. Because, you know, while it's happening, like I said, I'm sort of detached, just watching myself do it. But the second I stop, the second I can't physically eat another bite, it's like all the reality of what I just did comes crashing down on me at once. 

I'll look at the wrappers on the counter, or the empty containers, and I just think, "What is wrong with you?" I mean, I'm a 42-year-old man. I have a degree. I should be able to control myself around a box of crackers or a carton of ice cream, right? But I can't. And then I start thinking about how much money I just wasted on food that I didn't even really taste or enjoy, because I was just shoveling it in. Working as a cashier, you know, money isn't exactly flowing like water, so every dollar counts. And then I think about how I'm going to feel the next day at work, standing there for eight hours feeling bloated and disgusted with myself. 

It just spirals. I'll sit there in the kitchen, sometimes for an hour, just beating myself up over it. I'll tell myself I'm weak, that I have no willpower, that I'm never going to get my life together if I can't even stop myself from eating an entire loaf of bread at midnight. It's just... it's a really dark place to be in. And the worst part is, I know I'm going to do it again. Even while I'm sitting there feeling so ashamed, I know that the next time I have a bad shift or a stressful dinner, I'll be right back in that same spot, doing the exact same thing. It makes me feel completely hopeless, honestly.
Do you feel like you're eating much more rapidly than usual during these episodes?

Yeah, I mean... I guess I do? It's hard to say exactly because, like I mentioned, I get so zoned out. But now that you bring it up, when I really think about the mechanics of it... I suppose I am. It's not like a normal meal where you sit down, you take a bite, you put your fork down, you take a sip of water, maybe think about your day. It’s nothing like that. It’s more like... a frantic kind of energy. 

I remember the other night, after a particularly awful Tuesday shift—Tuesdays are the worst because we get the delivery truck in and everyone is always so on edge—I came home and I had this bag of chips. And I wasn't just eating them, I was practically inhaling them. I’d grab a handful, and before I even really finished chewing the first handful, my other hand was already reaching back into the bag for the next one. It’s like this weird assembly line in my head where the only goal is to get the food from the container into my mouth as fast as physically possible. 

And it’s so strange because I don't even really taste it. You'd think if you're eating that much, you'd want to enjoy the flavor, right? Especially with the good stuff, like the expensive cookies I sometimes buy when I get my paycheck. But no, it's just... crunch, swallow, grab more. Crunch, swallow, grab more. Sometimes I even scrape the roof of my mouth because I'm eating so fast and not chewing properly, like with crusty bread or something. I'll wake up the next morning and my mouth will actually be sore, and I'll think, "Why on earth did I do that?" But in the moment, it just feels like if I don't eat it as fast as I can, something terrible is going to happen. Or maybe it's just that I want to get it over with? I don't know. It’s just this desperate, rushed feeling, like I'm running out of time, even though I'm just standing alone in my own kitchen at one in the morning with absolutely nowhere to be.
How often do these eating episodes happen, would you say they occur at least once a week?

Well, yeah, I'd say so. At least once a week, for sure. It's been going on like this for the last few months, honestly. It seems like every week, I'll have at least one of those nights where I just completely lose it in the kitchen. Sometimes it's a Tuesday, like I was saying about the delivery truck, but other times it could be a Friday when I'm just so exhausted from the whole week that my defenses are totally down. 

And the thing is, it's not just the eating part that happens every week. It's the whole... cycle of it. Because after I do it, after I eat all that food and feel so incredibly full and sick and disgusted with myself, I panic. I just panic about the weight I'm going to gain, about how my uniform pants are already tight enough, and how I can't afford to buy new ones on a cashier's salary. So I feel like I have to fix it, you know? I have to undo what I just did. 

So, for the last few months, almost every time I have one of those out-of-control nights, I end up trying to make up for it. Sometimes I'll go to the bathroom and force myself to throw up, which is just... it's horrible, it really is. My throat burns, my eyes water, and I just feel so pathetic kneeling there. But in the moment, it feels like the only way to get the food out of me. Or if I don't do that, I'll take a bunch of laxatives before I go to sleep, hoping that'll flush it all out. Which, let me tell you, makes the next shift at work absolute torture, constantly worrying if I need to run to the restroom while there's a line of five people waiting to pay. 

And if I can't bring myself to do either of those things, I'll just refuse to eat the entire next day. I'll skip breakfast, skip my lunch break—I'll just drink black coffee and tell my coworkers I have a stomach bug if they ask why I'm not eating. Or I'll force myself to go on this massive, punishing walk after my shift. I'm talking miles and miles, until my feet are blistered and my calves are screaming, just trying to burn off every single calorie from the night before. So, yeah, this whole exhausting routine... the eating, and then the throwing up, or the pills, or the starving, or the walking... it's definitely been happening most weeks for the last few months now. It's like a second job I didn't sign up for.
Do you think your actions after these eating episodes, like throwing up or taking laxatives, are helping you avoid gaining weight?

Yeah, I mean... that is exactly what I tell myself in the moment. I look at it like a reset button, I guess? Which sounds completely ridiculous when I actually say it out loud to you. But there have been times, you know, usually late at night after everyone else in the house finally goes to bed and it is just me awake. The house gets completely quiet, and I will just sort of creep into the bathroom. I always make sure to turn on the exhaust fan or run the faucet so nobody hears anything, and I will make myself throw up. Or I will take those laxatives I mentioned. And the whole time, the entire time I am doing it, I am just playing this constant loop in my head, telling myself that it is fine, that I am just undoing the damage. I literally use those exact words in my head—undoing the damage. I try to convince myself that I am just getting rid of the calories so I don't gain weight, so I don't have to face the physical consequences of what I just shoved into my body. 

But then... the reality of it actually hits me. Because it does not feel like a neat little solution afterward. Not at all. When it is over, I will just sit there on the cold bathroom tiles, and I feel so incredibly shaky. Like, physically, my hands will be trembling, my legs feel like jelly, and my heart is just pounding in my chest. And the embarrassment... God, the embarrassment is just suffocating. I will splash cold water on my face and look at myself in the mirror, and I just think about how I am a 42-year-old man with a college degree, sneaking around a bathroom in the middle of the night doing this to myself. I just feel so deeply embarrassed and pathetic. 

So, do I think it helps? In that desperate, panicked moment, my brain tricks me into thinking it is saving me from gaining weight. But physically and emotionally, it just leaves me a shaky, humiliated mess. It is like I am just trading the guilt of eating for the shame of... well, of getting rid of it. And I just sit there on the floor, shivering, wondering how my life ended up looking like this.
Do you feel like you would still try to throw up or use laxatives after these eating episodes even if you didn't worry about gaining weight?

If I didn't worry about gaining weight? That's... I mean, I don't even know how to picture that, to be honest. It's like asking if I'd still wear a raincoat if it never rained. Because, no, absolutely not. I really don't think I would. I mean, why would I? 

Like I was saying before, making myself throw up is just an awful, awful experience. It's not something I do for fun, or because I like the feeling of it. God, no. The acid burns my throat, my eyes get all red and puffy, and my nose runs. Sometimes I even get these little broken blood vessels around my eyelids from the strain, which I then have to try and hide the next day at work, just praying the customers don't look too closely at me while I'm scanning their groceries. And the laxatives... I mean, who in their right mind would willingly put themselves through those terrible stomach cramps if they didn't feel absolutely terrified of the alternative? The cramps are like someone is twisting a hot knife in my gut. 

So, no, if I somehow magically woke up tomorrow and just didn't care at all about the number on the scale, or if my uniform pants fit, or if my face looked bloated... if all that worry just vanished? I would never kneel in front of that toilet again. I would just eat the food and... I guess I'd just let it sit there. 

Which, I mean, being overly full is uncomfortable, sure. Sometimes my stomach gets so tight after I eat like that, it actually aches, and I have to lie on my left side on the couch just to relieve the pressure. So I guess there is a physical discomfort to the fullness itself, but... no, I wouldn't go to these miserable extremes just for that. The only reason I put myself through this whole humiliating routine, the only reason I sneak around my own house like a criminal in the middle of the night, is because I am just so paralyzed by the thought of gaining weight. If you took that fear away... I'd have no reason to do it. At least, I really don't think I would. It's just hard to completely separate the two in my head, you know? Because the fear of the weight is just always, always there.
Do you think you would still feel the need to binge eat if you didn't worry about gaining weight?

That’s... wow, um, that’s a really tough question to wrap my head around. Because, well, I honestly don't know. I really don't. I'm trying to just sit here and picture it, you know, a version of me that just completely doesn't care about gaining weight, and my mind just sort of goes blank. Because the two things—the eating and the worrying—they are just so completely tangled up together in my brain right now. Like, I’ll be at work, just doing my normal routine, scanning groceries, bagging things up, and even when I'm just looking at the food coming down the conveyor belt, the weight worry is just always humming there in the background. 

So when I get home, and I have one of those nights where I just lose control in the kitchen... is the urge to eat like that completely separate from the weight stuff? I mean, I genuinely couldn't tell you. Sometimes I think I just do it because I'm so incredibly stressed out and exhausted. You know, standing on my feet for eight hours straight, dealing with people who want to yell at me because their twenty-cent coupon expired a year ago... by the time I get home, I just want to completely numb out. I just want to shut my brain off, and the food does that for a few minutes. But even then, the fear of the weight is just lurking right there, waiting to pounce the second I stop chewing. 

So if you completely removed the fear of gaining weight... would I still have that desperate need to just eat everything in sight? I really, truly don't know. I've never experienced the urge to eat without the panic being attached to it, at least not for a very long time. It’s like trying to imagine a completely different life, honestly. I wish I could give you a simple yes or no, I really do, but I just... I haven't ever noticed what it feels like to just have one without the other.
Do you think the urge to binge eat is triggered by the stressful events of your day, regardless of the potential weight gain?

Well, that's... that's kind of the main thing that actually brought me in here to see you in the first place, to be honest. It's that feeling of just... completely losing the reins. Like, yes, the stress is definitely a huge part of it. I'll come home from the store, and maybe I had a really awful shift, or maybe I just had a really tense dinner with my family where everyone was kind of snapping at each other, and I'll just feel so wound up. My shoulders will be up around my ears, and my jaw is clenched so tight my teeth actually ache. 

And then I'll start eating. Maybe I just tell myself I'm going to have a handful of chips, or a couple of cookies to just sort of take the edge off, you know? Just to unwind for a second. But then... it's like a switch flips in my brain. It's the most terrifying feeling, really. It's like the logical, decision-making part of my brain just completely powers down. It just shuts right off. 

I'll literally be standing there in the kitchen, and I can actually see my own hand reaching into the cabinet for another box of crackers, or grabbing a loaf of bread, and it's like I'm watching myself do it from the outside. I know I shouldn't be doing it. I know I'm already full, I know I'm going to feel terrible and guilty and panicked about the weight later, but in that exact moment, I just... I can't make myself stop. It's like my body has been hijacked. I'll just keep opening packages, and chewing, and swallowing, and the whole time my brain is just screaming at me to stop, but my hands just keep moving. It's just this total, complete loss of control, regardless of what the scale is going to say tomorrow. That feeling of being totally powerless while I'm doing it... that's what really scares me the most.
Do you think you would still feel the urge to binge eat after a stressful event if you knew you couldn't gain weight from it?

If I knew for a hundred percent certainty that I wouldn't gain a single pound? Man... I mean, the urge is just so incredibly strong when I'm stressed. It's like a tidal wave. I think... I think I probably still would have that urge, because of just how intense the compulsion gets and just the sheer volume of what I'm eating when I'm in that zone. 

Like, to give you an idea of what I'm actually doing when I lose control like that... on bad nights, I can come home and just demolish a full plate of leftovers from the fridge. Like, whatever is in there, maybe a huge portion of pasta or whatever, just gone. And you'd think that would be enough, right? That would be a normal dinner for anyone else. But I just keep going. I'll just stand there in the kitchen, and within an hour or two, I'm going through bread, just shoving slices in my mouth, and then whatever snacks I can find in the pantry, and then I'm digging into the ice cream in the freezer. 

It's just this massive, massive amount of food. It's way, way more than I’d ever eat if someone were sitting with me, you know? Like, if a friend was hanging out at my place, or if my mom was visiting, I would never in a million years eat like that in front of them. I'd be absolutely mortified. But when I'm alone and that stress from the store just boils over... it's like a bottomless pit. So, yeah, I think that drive to just stuff down the stress with all those leftovers and snacks and ice cream, that desperate attempt to just numb my brain with food... it might still happen even without the weight fear, just because the habit of using all that food to cope with a bad day is so deeply ingrained in me now.
Do you think the binge eating itself is the main problem you're trying to solve, rather than the potential weight gain that follows?

I mean... honestly? I think they’re neck and neck, but the weight gain... man, the fear of the weight gain is what really tortures me the most the next day. It’s like the binge is the crime, and the weight panic is the punishment, and the punishment just lasts so much longer. Because, see, I have this routine, right? I get up, and before I even shower or have a sip of coffee or anything, I step on the scale in my bathroom. 

And if that number... if the scale is even a pound higher in the morning, just one single pound, I get this overwhelming, panicky feeling. It just drops my stomach right out. It's this absolute terror that I’m just sliding into being fat, you know? Like that one pound is the start of this unstoppable avalanche and I'm just going to keep expanding.

And that panic, it doesn't just stay in the bathroom. It completely ruins my entire day and dictates everything I do. Like, my family gets together a lot, and if we have a family meal that day, I’ll show up and I just... I start avoiding rice, or anything oily, or really anything that looks heavy. My mom will put these big, rich dishes out, and I'll just take the driest, plainest thing I can find, and I'll avoid the rice completely, just pushing food around my plate. 

And the really frustrating part is, I *know* it's irrational. I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I'm a smart enough guy, I know perfectly well that one meal shouldn't matter that much in the grand scheme of things. I know a single pound on the scale is probably just water retention or something. But that logical part of my brain just gets totally shouted down by the panic. I'll just sit there at the table with my family, terrified of the oil on the vegetables, terrified of the rice, just totally consumed by it. So... yeah, the bingeing is an awful loss of control, but that lingering, obsessive terror about gaining weight... that's the part that feels like it's really running—and ruining—my life.
Do you think your binge eating episodes would decrease in frequency if you found healthier ways to cope with stress?

I mean, logically? Yes, probably. If I could just... I don't know, do some deep breathing or meditate or something after a bad shift at the register instead of tearing through the kitchen, I'm sure it would help. But it's just... it's become this whole vicious cycle, you know? It's not just a standalone event where I get stressed, I eat, and then it's over and I can just try a new coping skill next time. It’s this whole exhausting production. 

Because if I really look back at, say, just the last few months? It’s been happening most weeks. Almost every single week I'll have one of those completely out-of-control eating nights. And the stress of the binge itself just creates a whole new level of panic for me, like I was saying before with the scale. So then I have to... I have to fix it, right? I have to undo what I just did because the thought of that weight gain is just screaming in my head. 

So to make up for it, I'll end up throwing up, or I'll take a bunch of laxatives just to empty myself out and try to feel normal again. Or, if I don't do that, I'll just completely skip meals the next day, just running on empty, or I'll force myself to go on this incredibly long, punishing walk around the neighborhood for hours until my feet are blistered and my legs are shaking. And then, by the time I've done all of *that* just to make up for the binge, I'm so physically and mentally drained that my stress levels are right back through the roof anyway. It just primes me to lose control all over again the next time a customer yells at me or my family gets tense. 

So, finding a healthier way to cope... I mean, it sounds great on paper, I really do want that, but I'm just so tangled up in this routine of eating and then frantically trying to erase the eating, I don't even know how to break out of the loop to try something else.
Do you think the stress from your daily life is more responsible for triggering your binge eating episodes than your fear of gaining weight?

I mean... gosh, that's a really tough question to untangle. Honestly, I really don't know which one is the bigger culprit. It's like asking about the chicken or the egg, you know? Because, on one hand, I have these days at the store... like just last Tuesday, the scanner at my lane was acting up, the lines were backing up all the way into the clothing aisles, and people get so incredibly impatient. And as a cashier, you're just standing there taking the brunt of all these heavy sighs and eye rolls and snide comments for eight hours straight. So by the time I clock out, my shoulders are practically up to my ears, my head is pounding, and all I want to do is go home and completely zone out with food. The stress is just so heavy, it feels like it's physically crushing my chest. 

But then... but then I think about the weight, right? Because even while I'm stressed and driving home from that awful shift, I'm already thinking about my body, and I'm already feeling this low-level hum of anxiety about getting fat. And sometimes I wonder if that constant anxiety about my weight actually makes the daily stress from work feel so much worse, or if the daily stress makes the fear of gaining weight worse. 

So, which one is actually more responsible for triggering me to lose control? I really couldn't tell you. I've tried to sit down and figure it out before, like, okay, am I doing this tonight because that lady yelled at me over an expired coupon, or am I doing this because I stepped on the scale this morning, saw a number I didn't like, and just felt completely hopeless about myself? And I just... I can't separate them anymore. They just bleed right into each other. It's this giant, messy knot in my head. I'll start analyzing it, thinking maybe it's definitely the job, but then I realize how much of my mental energy every single day is spent just being utterly terrified of my waistline, and I just get totally lost in the weeds trying to parse it out. I wish I could give you a clear-cut answer, like it's sixty percent the job and forty percent the scale, but I really just don't know. They're just both constantly there, buzzing in the background, all day long.
Do you think you would still try to purge after binge eating if you didn't have any fear of gaining weight?

I mean... wow, if you completely removed the fear of gaining weight? That’s... that’s hard to even imagine, because that fear is just so baked into the whole process for me. But if I really try to picture it, if I magically didn't care about my weight at all... I honestly don't think I would go through with it. Because the whole reason I do it, the whole justification in my head, is entirely about the weight. 

Like, I have this whole secret routine, right? It usually happens late at night. I'll wait until the house is completely quiet, after everyone goes to bed, and I'm just sitting there in the dark feeling so incredibly full and panicked about what I just ate. And that's when I'll sneak off to the bathroom, trying to be as quiet as possible so nobody hears the floorboards creak, and I... I make myself throw up. Or, if I can't bring myself to do that, I'll take a bunch of laxatives. And the entire time I'm in there doing it, I'm just playing this mental tape on a loop, telling myself over and over that it’s just to undo the damage. That's the exact phrase I use in my head: "undo the damage." And by damage, I mean the calories, the fat, the pound on the scale the next morning. If I didn't care about the weight, there wouldn't *be* any damage to undo, you know? 

Because, I'll tell you, it's not like I actually want to be doing it. It's awful. Every single time, right afterward, I'm just sitting there on the bathroom floor, leaning against the cold porcelain of the bathtub or the sink, and I feel so incredibly embarrassed. I'll catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror, my eyes all watery, and just feel this massive wave of shame about what a 42-year-old man with a college degree is doing in the middle of the night. And physically, I feel terrible too—I get all shaky and weak, my hands will literally be trembling while I'm rinsing out my mouth, and I have to splash cold water on my face just to pull myself together before I creep back to bed. 

It’s this incredibly draining, humiliating experience. So, yeah, if I didn't have that absolute terror of waking up heavier, I can't imagine I'd ever put myself through all that shaking and embarrassment. The fear of the weight is the only thing that drives me to try and erase the food... if that makes sense? I just... I get so caught up in trying to fix the mistake, but the mistake is only a mistake because of the scale.
Would you still feel the need to purge after eating if you knew you couldn't gain weight from it?

I mean, yeah, like I was kind of saying just a minute ago... if I knew for an absolute fact that I couldn't gain weight from it? I definitely wouldn't do it. Because right now, my whole life is just completely dictated by this constant terror of getting bigger. It's exhausting just thinking about it. 

Like, just to give you an idea of how deep this goes for me... every single morning, the very first thing I do is check my weight. And if the scale is even a pound higher in the morning—just one single pound!—I get this horrible, panicky feeling right in my chest. It’s this overwhelming dread that I’m just sliding into being fat, like I'm losing all control and it's just a slippery slope from there. 

And that panic, it just completely takes over everything I do. It’s why I try to undo the binges, of course, but it even messes up totally normal situations. Like... well, like family dinners. If I've had a bad morning on the scale, or if I'm feeling that panic, I'll go to a family meal and I'll start completely avoiding the rice, or I'll refuse to touch anything that looks even slightly oily. My family will make these big spreads and I'm just sitting there analyzing every grain of rice on the table, absolutely terrified of it. And the most frustrating part is that I *know* better. I really do! I'm an educated guy, I know logically that one meal shouldn’t matter that much in the grand scheme of things. I know a scoop of rice isn't going to suddenly pack on ten pounds. But I just can't shake that screaming thought in my head that if I eat the oily food, I'm going to get fat. 

So, yeah, if you could just wave a magic wand and guarantee I wouldn't gain weight from eating? The purging would stop immediately. I wouldn't need to do it at all. The only reason I put myself through all that misery in the bathroom is just a desperate attempt to stop that scale from moving up the next morning, so I don't have to feel that horrible panic.
Do you think your need to purge after binge eating is solely driven by your fear of gaining weight?

I mean, yeah, honestly... like I was just saying a minute ago, it really is one hundred percent that fear. I know I'm repeating myself a bit here, but it's just so central to the whole thing. Because, like I described, when I'm actually in the middle of it—when I wait for everyone to go to bed, and the house is dead quiet, and I'm in the bathroom making myself throw up, or when I'm taking those laxatives—the only thing I'm trying to accomplish is to undo the damage. That’s the only goal. 

There's no other benefit to it, you know? It's not like it feels good or gives me some kind of high. It's actually the exact opposite. The physical act itself is just... it's so incredibly unpleasant. I get so horribly shaky afterward, like my blood sugar is crashing or something, and my whole body is just vibrating and weak. And the embarrassment is just... it's overwhelming. I'm sitting there on the floor, wiping my mouth, feeling so much shame about what I've just done. 

If there was literally any other reason behind it, I feel like I wouldn't be able to tolerate how awful and embarrassing the whole ordeal is. I'd just stop. But because I am so absolutely terrified of what's going to happen to my body if I digest that food, I push through all that physical shakiness and all that humiliation just to get rid of it. I tell myself, over and over, "you just have to undo the damage, you have to fix this." So, yes, to answer your question, it really is solely driven by that fear. If you took the fear of the weight away, there is no way on earth I would put myself through all that misery in the middle of the night.
Do you think your binge eating episodes would happen even if you didn't have the fear of gaining weight, but still experienced the same level of stress in your daily life?

That's... wow, that's a really interesting question, actually. Because, you know, we've been talking so much about the fear of the weight and the bathroom stuff, but the eating part... the eating part feels almost like a totally separate beast. 

If I still had the same amount of stress in my life? Yeah. Yeah, I think the eating would absolutely still happen. Because... well, let me explain what it's actually like when it starts. Honestly, this is really what brought me in to see you in the first place. It's because of how the eating itself actually happens. 

I work as a cashier, right? Which, you know, I'm a 42-year-old man, I have a bachelor's degree, and here I am ringing people up all day, dealing with all these frustrated, sometimes completely unreasonable customers, standing on my feet for eight hours... it just builds up this incredible amount of tension. Or even just after a really tense dinner, like those family meals I mentioned before. I'll get home, or I'll finally be alone, and my stress levels are just completely through the roof, my shoulders are practically up to my ears. 

And I'll start eating. Just to, I don't know, decompress or quiet my mind for a second? But then... it's like a switch flips in my head. It literally feels like the decision-making part of me just completely shuts off. It's the most bizarre, overwhelming feeling. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, and it’s almost like an out-of-body experience. Like I can physically see my own hand reaching into the pantry, grabbing more food, tearing open another package, and my logical brain is somewhere way in the background shouting, "What are you doing? You're not even hungry, put it down!" but... I just can't make myself stop. 

It’s like the stress just completely overloads my circuits, and once I take those first few bites to cope with it, the brakes just completely give out. I become a passenger in my own body. So even if I wasn't terrified of the scale the next morning, that feeling of just completely losing the ability to stop myself... that would still be there, as long as the stress is there. The stress starts it, and then that total loss of control takes over. It's like I'm on autopilot and someone else is flying the plane, you know? I just keep eating and eating, totally disconnected from any rational thought until I'm physically uncomfortable...
Do you think your binge eating episodes are more often triggered by your daily stress or your fear of gaining weight?

Honestly, it's definitely the stress that triggers the eating part. The fear of gaining weight, that's what makes me panic *after* the fact, but the stress is what starts the whole avalanche. 

Because when I get home from the store, you know, and my feet are just throbbing from standing on that hard floor all day, and I've just had it with people complaining about coupons or prices... I just need an escape. My brain is just fried. And that's when the eating happens.
